title: Tallahassee Armed Drug Trafficker Sentenced to 25 Years in Federal Prison
body: Press Release Tallahassee Armed Drug Trafficker Sentenced to 25 Years in Federal Prison Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Tallahassee, Florida – Christopher L. Daniels, 47, of Tallahassee, Florida, was sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty by a federal jury of possession with intent to distribute various controlled substances including more than 50 grams of methamphetamine, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This serial felon made a career out of victimizing our communities and flooding our streets with deadly poison, but thanks to the aggressive prosecution by my office he’ll spend decades behind federal bars where he belongs. This case was built upon the close cooperation between the Tallahassee Police Department, ATF, and DEA, and shows our unified commitment to dismantling and eradicating the drug trafficking operations that have plagued our neighborhoods with violence, addiction, and blight. Our citizens deserve to live in safe, drug-free communities, and my office will deliver on that promise with aggressive prosecutions and lengthy prison sentences for anyone caught breaking the law in my District.” Evidence at trial demonstrated that the Tallahassee Police Department conducted an investigation into drug trafficking by the defendant that culminated in the execution of a search warrant at his home on January 21, 2026. Officers found approximately 2.75 ounces of methamphetamine, an ounce of cocaine, half an ounce of crack cocaine laid out in plain view on an ironing board, approximately one ounce of “molly” (two different synthetic cathinones), 64 suspected MDMA tablets later confirmed to be low-purity methamphetamine, and a pound of marijuana. Four pistols were also found in the house, including a “Draco” AK-47-style pistol found near the plate of crack cocaine. Evidence on the defendant’s cellphone showed that he was engaged in drug-trafficking. The defendant is a 12-time convicted felon, with convictions dating back to 1996, and faced enhanced sentencing due to multiple prior convictions for serious drug felonies. “North Florida residents are much safer today,” said ATF Tampa Field Division’s Special Agent in Charge Kirk Howard. “Special thanks to Tallahassee Police Department, DEA and federal prosecutors for holding this repeat violent offender accountable.” This sentencing was the result of a joint investigation by the Tallahassee Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration. Assistant United States Attorney James A. McCain prosecuted the case. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities . title: LOUISIANA UNITED: THREE DISTRICTS, ONE MISSION CONFERENCE & CLE BRINGS FEDERAL AND STATE PARTNERS TOGETHER IN NEW ORLEANS
body: Press Release LOUISIANA UNITED: THREE DISTRICTS, ONE MISSION CONFERENCE & CLE BRINGS FEDERAL AND STATE PARTNERS TOGETHER IN NEW ORLEANS Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Louisiana On November 5-6, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Offices in the Eastern, Middle, and Western Districts of Louisiana gathered in New Orleans for a first-of-its-kind event: a two-day collaboration titled Louisiana United: Three Districts, One Mission CLE and Conference consisting of trainings and seminars dedicated to advancing the shared principles of law, justice, and public safety throughout our State. The three United States Attorneys in Louisiana—David I. Courcelle for the Eastern District, Kurt L. Wall for the Middle District, and Zachary A. Keller for the Western District—share one unified statement about the value of this gathering: “ Louisiana United is more than a professional development conference. It is a symbol of our three Offices’ shared commitment to the safety and well-being of the people of Louisiana. Our Offices work tirelessly every single day to create safer communities in our respective Districts, and our hope is that collaboration like this will help each Office to better serve by sharing ideas and learning new and more effective ways to serve our communities.” The event opened with a welcoming address from United States Attorney General Todd Blanche, followed by an address by the Director of the Executive Office of the United States Attorneys, Francey Hakes and Deputy Director Scott Laragy. From there, the conference featured presentations and roundtable discussions that featured Assistant United States Attorneys, federal judges, Department of Justice leadership, and professional staff from across the state. Attendees participated in continuing legal education and professional development programs, addressing issues such as governmental ethics, trial advocacy, appeals, effective communication, and interagency collaboration, and others. A highlight of the conference was the participation of distinguished members of the federal judiciary from across the state, including Chief United States District Judge Wendy B. Vitter; United States District Judges Lance M. Africk, Jay C. Zainey, and Brandon S. Long of the Eastern District; United States District Judge Brian A. Jackson of the Middle District; and United States District Judges Jerry Edwards, Jr., Alexander C. Van Hook, and David C. Joseph of the Western District. Through panel discussions and presentations, the judges shared their insights on professionalism, effective advocacy, legal writing, courtroom practice, and emerging issues facing federal practitioners. The event concluded with a distinguished panel discussion on federal-state partnerships featuring Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, Louisiana District Attorneys Association President Perry Nicosia, 22nd JDC District Attorney Collin Sims, and Louisiana Legislative Auditor Michael J. Waguespack. Panelists discussed the importance of cooperation among federal, state, and local partners in promoting public safety, accountability, and the rule of law. Louisiana United: Three Districts, One Mission is a collaborative professional development and Continuing Legal Education conference bringing together U.S. Attorneys Offices in the Eastern, Middle, and Western Districts of Louisiana. The conference promotes professional excellence, collaboration, and leadership—and a unified commitment to law, justice, and public safety throughout Louisiana. title: Gainesville Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Child Exploitation Charges After Video Recording in Public Restrooms
body: Press Release Gainesville Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Child Exploitation Charges After Video Recording in Public Restrooms Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Gainesville, Florida – Bryan James Shuping, 58, of Gainesville, Florida has pleaded guilty in federal court in Gainesville to one count of production of child pornography and one count of possessing child pornography. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida, announced the guilty plea. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Keeping our kids safe from disgusting sexual predators, like this defendant, is of paramount importance to me and my office. We will continue to aggressively prosecute these crimes to ensure he and others like him remain locked away behind federal bars for as long as possible.” Court records reflect that on multiple occasions from June 18, 2025, to August 2, 2025, the defendant entered men’s public bathrooms at the Oaks Mall and Depot Park in Gainesville, Florida, and filmed minors as they used the bathroom. The videos and images that the defendant produced were of the minors with their genitals exposed while they were attempting to use the bathroom. The defendant admitted that this was done for sexual gratification. The defendant also admitted to possessing other images of child pornography that he had downloaded from the internet. The defendant faces a minimum mandatory 15 years up to life imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for February 16, 2027, at 10:30 a.m. at the United States Courthouse in Gainesville, Florida before Chief United States District Judge Allen C. Winsor. This case is being jointly investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Tyler Fleming. If you have information regarding nonconsensual filming of minors during the dates and locations listed above please contact Homeland Security Investigations by email at NDFL_HSI_Gainesville@ice.dhs.gov . This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . title: Hulbert Resident Pleads Guilty To Making False Declarations Before Grand Jury
body: Press Release Hulbert Resident Pleads Guilty To Making False Declarations Before Grand Jury Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Oklahoma MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Stephanie Jane Thompson, age 49, of Hulbert, Oklahoma, entered a guilty plea to one count of False Declarations Before Grand Jury, punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The Superseding Indictment alleged that on January 13, 2026, Thompson knowingly made a false material declaration while under oath and testifying in a proceeding before a Grand Jury of the United States in the Eastern District of Oklahoma. The charge arose from an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Fort Gibson Police Department, the Hulbert Police Department, the Cherokee County Sheriff’s Office, the Cherokee Nation Marshal Service, the Oklahoma Highway Patrol, and the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation. The Honorable D. Edward Snow, Magistrate Judge in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, accepted the plea and ordered the completion of a presentence investigation report. A U.S. District Court Judge will determine the sentence to be imposed after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Thompson will remain on bond with conditions of pretrial release pending sentencing. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan E. Soverly represented the United States. Hickey presided over the sentencing hearing in the United States District Court, at El Dorado. On or about May 27, 2026, Johnson pleaded guilty in federal court to both Possession of Cocaine with the Intent to Distribute and possession of firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking. title: Murder on the high seas: alleged cruise ship killer gets federal charges
body: Press Release Murder on the high seas: alleged cruise ship killer gets federal charges Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Texas GALVESTON, Texas – A 48-year-old Tyler resident has been taken into custody on charges of murder. Jason Watford is set to make his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew Edison in Galveston at 1 p.m. The charges allege that on Nov. 8, Watford struck a female passenger several times before strangling her with his hands and arm following a dispute in their room while aboard a cruise ship in international waters. According to the criminal complaint, Watford and the woman had been dining at a restaurant aboard the ship when they began to argue. The charges allege he left and went to their room, followed by the woman approximately 25 minutes later. At approximately 9 p.m., less than an hour after the woman had entered the room, a cruise ship housekeeper knocked on the door and spoke briefly with Watford, according to the allegations. She allegedly noticed blood on his hands and clothing, saw the woman lying face down and motionless on the floor, and alerted personnel. They found the woman deceased with multiple facial injuries, according to the charges. The complaint further alleges no one else had been seen entering or exiting the room during that time. If convicted, Watford faces up to life in prison as well as a possible $250,000 maximum fine. FBI – Texas City Resident Agency is conducting the investigation with the assistance of U.S. Coast Guard, Port of Galveston Police Department, Customs and Border Protection, and the cruise ship company. Assistant U.S. Attorney Anh-Khoa Tran is prosecuting the case. A criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law. Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - Texas, Southern

title: Arizona Federal Court Denies Request to Halt Hermosa Critical Minerals Project
body: Press Release Arizona Federal Court Denies Request to Halt Hermosa Critical Minerals Project Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona last week denied a motion for a preliminary injunction to halt construction of the Hermosa Critical Minerals Project in southeastern Arizona. The project will establish a domestic source of manganese and substantially increase domestic production of zinc, which are essential to the steel used in military vehicles and naval vessels. In battery-grade form, manganese is also essential to the advanced lithium-ion batteries that power unmanned aerial vehicles, radios, and other defense equipment. The United States relies entirely on imports of manganese and almost entirely on imports of zinc, with China providing about 95% of global refining capacity for manganese used in advanced batteries. “Manganese is indispensable to our national defense, and the United States cannot afford to remain dependent on foreign supply chains,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of the Justice Department’s Energy and Natural Resources Division (ENRD). “This ruling allows work to proceed on the only domestic project positioned to produce battery-grade manganese. The Department will continue to defend agency action to restart domestic production of critical minerals.” After roughly three years of environmental review, the U.S. Forest Service approved the Hermosa project in July 2026. The project expands existing mining operations on private land onto the Coronado National Forest. The approval followed formal consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under the Endangered Species Act and imposes more than 400 binding design features, mitigation measures, and other conditions to minimize environmental impacts. To accelerate manganese and zinc production and refining, the Department of War has awarded the project $20 million under the Defense Production Act and the Department of Energy awarded $166.2 million. In late October, two environmental groups challenged the agencies’ decisions and asked the court to halt the project while the case proceeds. The court denied that motion because the plaintiffs had not shown they were likely to succeed on their claims. The plaintiffs also had not made the required showing of likely irreparable harm. Finally, the court recognized “a substantial public interest in domestic critical-mineral supply” and noted that “the national security interests are relevant and substantial.” As a result of the ruling, the approved work on the Project can proceed while the court considers the merits of the case on an expedited schedule. Attorneys with ENRD’s Wildlife and Marine Resources Section and Natural Resources Section are handling this matter. Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Environment Components Energy and Natural Resources Division ENRD - Natural Resources Section ENRD - Wildlife and Marine Resources Section Press Release Number: 26-1339

title: Pushmataha County Resident Pleads Guilty To Two Counts Of Assault With Intent To Do Bodily Harm
body: Press Release Pushmataha County Resident Pleads Guilty To Two Counts Of Assault With Intent To Do Bodily Harm Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Oklahoma MUSKOGEE, OKLAHOMA – The United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Oklahoma announced that Parker Kyle Taylor, age 34, of Fort Towson, Oklahoma, entered a guilty plea to two counts of Assault with a Dangerous Weapon with Intent to Do Bodily Harm in Indian Country, each punishable by up to ten years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The Indictment alleged that on or about July 26, 2026, Taylor assaulted one victim with a knife with intent to do bodily harm, then assaulted a responding deputy with a knife, intending to do bodily harm. The crimes occurred in Pushmataha County, within the boundaries of the Choctaw Nation Reservation, in the Eastern District of Oklahoma. The charges arose from an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation, and the Pushmataha County Sheriff’s Office. The Honorable Jason A. Robertson, Magistrate Judge in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, accepted the plea and ordered the completion of a presentence investigation report. A U.S. District Court Judge will determine the sentence to be imposed after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Taylor will remain in the custody of the United States Marshals Service pending sentencing. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Edith A. Singer and Kristin Knutson represented the United States. body: Press Release Detroit Man Sentenced to 14+ Years in Prison for Coercion, Enticement, and Child Pornography Charges Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Ohio TOLEDO, Ohio – A 40-year-old man has been sentenced to federal prison for arranging to engage in illicit sexual conduct with purported minor children and for Child Sexual Abuse Materials (CSAM) charges. Brett Tooman, of Detroit, Michigan, was sentenced to 174 months (14.5 years) in prison by U.S. District Judge James R. Knepp II, after pleading guilty to: •    Coercion or Enticement of a Minor •    Travel with Intent to Engage in Illicit Sexual Conduct •    Transportation of Child Pornography, or CSAM •    Receipt and Distribution of Child Pornography, or CSAM Tooman was also ordered to serve 25 years of supervised release after imprisonment, pay $37,500 in restitution, and to pay $5,000 toward the Justice for Victims of Trafficking Act, which was established in 2015 to provide justice for victims of trafficking. According to court documents, law enforcement was investigating suspected Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) activity on an online platform and Tooman was subsequently identified. Tooman was communicating online with an undercover agent who purportedly had minor children. Tooman expressed a strong desire to meet with the children in person to engage in sexual activity. After explicit and graphic communications with the undercover agent, Tooman agreed to meet the undercover agent and the purported children at a pre-arranged location. There, Tooman was immediately taken into custody by law enforcement officers. The investigation was led by the FBI Toledo Resident Agency’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force and the Toledo Police Department. Assistant United States Attorneys Sara Al-Sorghali and Alissa Sterling led the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. The initiative is led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, visit justice.gov/PSC. To report child exploitation, please visit cybertipline.org , or call 1-800-843-5678, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Contact Jessica Salas Novak Jessica.Salas.Novak@usdoj.gov Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Ohio, Northern

body: Waze Waze and Garmin team up to boost driver awareness of cyclists. Nov 10, 2026 Waze and Garmin are launching real-time cycling alerts to help create a safer environment on the road. Now, when cyclists turn on Garmin LiveTrack™ on their Garmin Edge® bike computer or Garmin smartwatch, they can choose to show up as a real-time, moving icon on Waze for extra peace of mind. Drivers will also see a notification when a cyclist is nearby, giving them a helpful reminder to slow down, stay aware, and share the road thoughtfully. This feature is completely opt-in and built with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby — never information about a specific cyclist or route. Plus, alerts automatically turn off the moment a cyclist ends their ride on their Garmin device. Cycling alerts powered by Garmin are rolling out now globally on Android and iOS.

title: Sioux Falls Man and Woman Sentenced to Lengthy Terms in Federal Prison  for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance
body: Press Release Sioux Falls Man and Woman Sentenced to Lengthy Terms in Federal Prison  for Conspiracy to Distribute a Controlled Substance Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota SIOUX FALLS - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a man and woman from Sioux Falls convicted of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance.  The sentencings took place on November 2, 2026. Julia Pewo, 63, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by five years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Coye Nohava, 42, was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison, followed by eight years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Pewo and Nohava were indicted for conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance by a federal grand jury in July 2025.  The defendants were found guilty following a 3-day jury trial ending August 13, 2026. Pewo and Nohava were sub-distributors in a conspiracy that was led by Matthew Shade in South Dakota. Shade worked with others in Arizona to obtain methamphetamine and transport it to South Dakota either through the mail or by vehicle.  Pewo and Nohava obtained methamphetamine from co-conspirators who were sourced by Shade and then distributed it to others.  Pewo was attributed with being involved in the distribution of approximately 13 pounds of methamphetamine and Nohava was attributed to 4 pounds. Nohava was also attributed with engaging in obstruction for committing perjury when he testified at trial in his defense. This case was investigated by the United States Postal Investigation Service, the Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Office, and the Sioux Falls Area Drug Task Force.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Hodges prosecuted the case. Pewo must self-surrender by noon on Friday, November 13, 2026. Nohava was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. Contact usasd.press@usdoj.gov Updated November 10, 2026 Topic Drug Trafficking Component USAO - South Dakota

title: Waller, The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism
body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 10, 2026 The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism Governor Christopher J. Waller At the Bank of England Watchers Conference  King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom Share Watch Live Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well. 1 My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term. The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy. At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening. 2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings. If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does. Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace. The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance. While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2 ). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low. These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking. This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged—it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market—there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable. The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy? The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier. I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure. So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications. One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post–World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent. 3 If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons. One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI. Another reason for low dynamism is that low firing may be a consequence of the huge surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023 related to the pandemic. Workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again, and that may be limiting job-switching. If this is a large factor, it may be temporary—workers are in their jobs for a median of three years before switching again, and we are nearing that threshold for the last of the pandemic job switchers. But it's possible they could be staying longer now if the job-switching triggered by the pandemic had been unusually effective at improving the matches between workers and jobs—many relocated or chased dreams and new careers and may not be as willing to switch again. As you can tell, it is hard to pin down and properly weigh the possible causes of lower labor market dynamism and then judge how long that phenomenon might continue. This makes it hard to know the implications for the economic outlook and monetary policy. But we can talk more constructively, I think, about the possible effects of the current low hire, low fire environment. While low layoffs imply that fewer workers experience unemployment, a low hiring rate means that those who do become unemployed may experience longer unemployment spells. And, in fact, the percentage of unemployed people who have been looking for work for more than six months has climbed steadily since 2022 and is now quite elevated for a period of economic expansion. 4 Another logical consequence of lower dynamism in the labor market would be that new entrants, typically young and with less experience, are having a harder time finding jobs. I think anyone paying attention to the U.S. economy has been hearing about the challenges young workers are facing. Indeed, the share of new labor force entrants in unemployment has been rising and has reached close to the highest levels of the past twenty years. Both these developments may reflect a labor market that is not as healthy as the headline unemployment rate indicates, with implications for the longer-term path of monetary policy. If hires and separations are low because worker matches have improved, then this may be a boost to productivity and can be largely ignored in assessing the state of the labor market. But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth. This possibility is important to monitor because productivity growth is a crucial factor in judging how fast the economy can grow without undesirable inflationary pressure. As I said earlier, I don't have the answers to the questions I have posed, but I believe the questions are worth asking and addressing with more research. Let me put aside this discussion about the health of the labor market for now. What is important in the near term is that I see the labor market as stable and employment at a level close to the FOMC's maximum-employment goal. By contrast, inflation is well above 2 percent and the focus of my attention. For reasons I explained at the start of this speech, I was willing to wait to tighten monetary policy at the FOMC's October meeting. Inconveniently for today's event, we will get consumer price index (CPI) inflation for October in a few hours. While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting. However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for. Let's just say it. September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining. Inflation based on personal consumption expenditures (PCE), the measure targeted by the FOMC, rose at a monthly rate of 0.5 percent in September and 3.7 percent over the previous 12 months. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September and 3.1 percent from that time last year. Both these measures are too high, and I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases. Earlier this year, excessive inflation was driven by nonmarket prices that are estimated rather than observed by the government, and ones that I tend to discount as hard to measure and as an unreliable guide to the overall trend for core inflation. But now, two components with greater relevance to future inflation are elevated—core goods prices and those for core market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of the components of core PCE service prices saw 12-month increases above 3 percent in September. Later today, I will be looking to see whether this breadth of elevated inflation continues, including whether high-tech goods prices related to the AI buildout continue to rise at the very high rate of recent months. I also want to know if the run-up in energy prices of the past several months is being passed through to goods and services directly or indirectly, because of higher input costs. While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained. Federal Reserve staff have been thinking hard about the effects on inflation of the AI buildout and elevated energy prices, and their findings do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon. In one exercise, researchers tried to capture imminent price pressures with a textual analysis of the well-known surveys of purchasing managers conducted by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM). 5 ISM surveys ask purchasing managers to list specific commodities, materials, and services whose prices rose or fell that month. 6 Staff used these responses to construct monthly price pressure indexes that correspond with actual categories of the producer price index (PPI). They found these indexes provide information about future changes in producer prices and, as a result, should have some signal about future PCE inflation. For example, the index for high-tech products rose in December 2025 and jumped further in January 2026, ahead of an escalation in those goods prices that eventually showed up in the February PPI and inflation data. The most recent ISM data, for October, point to the possibility of more price increases ahead. Some other Fed research indicates to me that energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past. 7 The researchers find a potential shift in the inflation process after the pandemic that suggests core inflation may be more responsive to energy shocks. Central bankers have tended to look through energy price shocks and expect that their effects on inflation will soon fade, but this new work cautions against taking too much comfort in this view. Their analysis suggests that, especially if oil prices were to remain elevated, these pressures could be larger than previously though and persist well into 2027. And there are reasons to also expect elevated energy prices to persist. First, even as there is increased tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, that traffic is moving at great expense. The insurance now needed for ships making this passing, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel. A second problem is that diesel oil production is affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints. As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East. To recap my economic outlook, economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC's 2 percent goal. This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting. That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Christopher J. Waller (2026), "The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections," speech delivered at the Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, Istanbul, October 8. For release at 4:00 p.m. EST Share The Federal Reserve Board on Monday announced its approval of two applications by Mutual Federal Bancorp, MHC, and MFB Bancorp, Inc., both of Chicago, Illinois. These approvals allow the banking organization to have a new top-tier holding company, MFB Bancorp, Inc., which would become a savings and loan holding company by acquiring Mutual Federal Bank, of Chicago, Illinois. title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)
body: AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026) Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist. The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines The new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed. To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2 . V2 is available in 10 Regions , and committed baseline pricing is coming soon. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena , Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio , or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written. Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize. AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode. AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday , Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge. AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub , with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS , and the new AgentCore Runtime. AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL. How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12). Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode. AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday , Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge. AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub , with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS , and the new AgentCore Runtime. AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL. How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12). Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
body: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation At the Conference on Robot Learning, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2, Isaac Lab 3.0 and new open benchmarks, built in collaboration with partners, bringing precision and scale to robot training. November 9, 2026 by Sasa Docca 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: GRAIL (Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning. RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies , which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency. These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment. NVIDIA is working with partners like Ambi Robotics , Bosch Research , Dexmate , Dyna Robotics , FieldAI , Flexion , Noitom Robotics , Siemens , Skild AI , RLWRLD , UC Berkeley , Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community. World Action Models Enable Next Level of Robot Autonomy The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2 , an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open source human egocentric data , the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include: Out-of-the-box performance: Completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. Skill transfer: Learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations Generalization with little data: Achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five. Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/groot-2-shipping-label.mp4 GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins. Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases. MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained. Training capable robots requires diverse data. Open NVIDIA workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation: For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a challenge inviting researchers to advance it. The NVIDIA EgoHand open model — being demoed at CoRL and with over 40,000 Hugging Face downloads in the two weeks since launch — reconstructs 3D hand motion, trained with data from Noitom Robotics . https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/egohand-demo.mp4 Where the Training and Scaling Happens — in Simulation A pretrained model gives robots a core set of skills. Simulation lets researchers train, refine and evaluate skills at scale before deploying them on physical robots. NVIDIA Isaac Lab , an open source robot-learning framework, provides the foundation for that work. Its latest release, Isaac Lab 3.0 , allows researchers to use agents to quickly set up training environments with simulation-ready assets , switch between NVIDIA PhysX and Newton physics solvers , choose renderers for perception-based training and apply a new reinforcement post-training library to foundation models like GR00T. Accurate physics is critical to transferring learned skills from simulation to the real robot. Tighter integration with Newton , an open source physics engine, now allows Isaac Lab to model deformable objects such as cables and cloth, along with complex articulated systems such as robotic hands with many interacting joints. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/newton-strawberry.mp4 Integration with Newton simulates how a strawberry deforms under a robot’s grip. Together, Isaac Lab and Newton combine accurate physics with scale to enable researchers to train thousands of simulated robots in parallel. In a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark, Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton achieved up to 2.5x the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/newton-physx-web.mp4 Isaac Lab supports robot simulation with Newton and NVIDIA PhysX. Developers are extending Newton’s capabilities. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/robotics-montage-8s.mp4 Skild AI’s STEEL Solver. Flexion showcased how Isaac Lab and Newton help train Reflect, its robot-intelligence model combining reasoning and whole-body manipulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/flexion-newton-isaac-lab.mp4 Flexion uses Newton for RL with Isaac Lab. FieldAI is using Newton — as well as Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries — to train and validate robot policies for deployment in unstructured real-world environments. Dyna Robotics will demonstrate how parallel simulation in Isaac Lab helps train whole-body controllers for its semi-humanoid Taku robot for work in warehouses, hotels and food services. Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics, while Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot. AlphaNIST , built in Isaac Lab, demonstrates how efficient practice can translate into precision. A single policy learns all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board, manipulating  millimeter-scale parts using only a yes-or-no success signal. It achieves more than 98% training success, compared with 81% for separate per-task policies, using roughly 39x less GPU time. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/alphanist-6-16s-web.mp4 AlphaNIST uses Isaac Lab to train a single robot policy across 20 precision tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board. Behind those results is Success-Guided Sampling , or SGS, from the University of Washington and NVIDIA. The method focuses practice on tasks a policy succeeds at about half the time, directing training toward skills it’s still learning. With SGS, robot training can scale beyond a million parallel environments. The University of Texas at Austin’s School of Computing and Texas Robotics uses Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to train robotic skills in simulation, letting students start developing before physical hardware is available. New Industrial Benchmarks for Robot Evaluation Learning a skill is one challenge. Performing it reliably across changing conditions is another. NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena , an open source framework for scaled policy evaluation, enables developers to compose diverse and repeatable evaluations, then run policies across thousands of variations in parallel. Analyses expose which conditions cause failures, so researchers know what to fix in their next training run. The developer preview of its latest version, 0.4, is arriving at CoRL. DexBench and VABAR, two new open benchmarks, are among the first designed to measure robot dexterity and adaptability across industrial tasks using Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton. DexBench , developed by RLWRLD in collaboration with NVIDIA, takes dexterity evaluation off the tabletop and into real-world workflows. Built using NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, it features 15 tasks across four scenes spanning retail, logistics, manufacturing and hospitality, testing generalization across object, spatial and physics variations. Genesis AI , mimic robotics and other industry partners are evaluating DexBench through early access. Teams can run DexBench on Manifold, Bifrost’s evaluation platform for scaling robotics simulations, with no setup required, built-in failure analysis and free credits for initial evaluations. VABAR — the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics — from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA, evaluates robots across six industrial tasks. Each carries standardized variations, difficulty tiers and success metrics. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/task-tool-sorting.mp4 A simulated tool-sorting task demonstrates how VABAR evaluates robot manipulation skills for industrial workflows. Agents Turn Skills Into Robot Programs Successful task completion requires robots to coordinate multiple skills and adapt when something goes wrong. Building reliable programs for these multistep tasks remains a challenge. Agentic robotics helps solve that challenge. UC Berkeley’s new Graph-as-Policy (GaP) framework uses agents to connect individual skills into robot programs. Agents test these programs using NVIDIA Isaac open simulation technologies and refine them based on failures. This helps researchers scale development with less data while keeping the programs interpretable for engineers to review and verify before deployment. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/wipe-the-bar.mp4 GaP uses agents and simulation to turn individual robot skills into coordinated actions, such as wiping a bar. “To me, agentic robotics is the most exciting technological development since the internet in 1995,” said Ken Goldberg, professor of robotics at UC Berkeley and a lead on the VABAR and GaP projects. Ambi Robotics is exploring GaP for industrial automation. Ambi Robotics , Bosch Research and Siemens are all exploring GaP for its agentic robotics workflows across diverse industrial scenarios. Learn more by joining NVIDIA at CoRL .
